narrative:
The model estimated a 61% chance that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. Because your law school application was tied to that prediction, this above-chance failure risk was the reason your application was rejected, even though a 61% estimate is not a certainty and leaves a meaningful possibility of passing.

The strongest driver was your third-year class standing. You were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile; this difference pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. Your LSAT score was the second most influential factor. At 37, it was very close to the accepted-student average of about 37.18, and it leaned slightly toward passing rather than failure. Your first-year standing was the third most important factor: you were in the second decile, compared with an accepted-student average near the sixth decile, and this also pushed the prediction toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.80 was strong relative to the accepted average of 3.23, but it was not among the top three factors in this decision.

Next, contact admissions to ask whether the decision can be reconsidered and what evidence would help. Focus on strengthening your academic record, especially your later-year performance, and seek bar-readiness advising. Retake the LSAT only if practice results show a clear gain; it was not the main weakness here.
